newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. overflight fees plan angers Canada airlines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. overflight fees plan angers Canada airlines.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration's move to charge planes for flying through U.S. airspace has raised concerns in the Canadian airline industry.

"We don't dispute the right of the U.S. to recover its costs. They're entitled to do that," said John Crichton, president of the Air Transport Association of Canada, which represents Canadian commercial air carriers.
"But there have been a whole bunch of important hoops that have been ignored here," Crichton said on Thursday in a phone interview. "What we strongly dispute is the process they've chosen."
The FAA said on Tuesday it plans to charge user fees to those aircraft flying through U.S. airspace that do not take off or land in the United States.

The FAA said the rule, which will be implemented on May 19, is consistent with international practices and is expected to recover about US$90 million in fee revenue for fiscal year 1998. Canada-to-Canada overflights in the United States have been granted deferral of the fees until October 1.
But Chrichton said the FAA has not followed international standards of consulting with users, discussing charges and providing notice of the changes.
"They should defer this," Crichton said. "It means tens of millions of dollars for Canadian air carriers."
Canada also charges for overflights, but U.S. aircraft that cross Canadian airspace on their way to another U.S. destination are exempt.
Canada's Transport Minister David Anderson plans to discuss the fees when he meets with U.S. Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater on Friday, a Transport Department spokesman said.
The spokesman would not confirm reports that Anderson will be asking for a partial exemption from the user fees.

Canada's airlines include the two main scheduled carriers - Air Canada and Canadian Airlines Corp, as well as charter airlines Transat A.T. Inc and Royal Aviation Inc. Many flights to destinations in Latin America and the Caribbean originating in Canada pass through U.S. airspace.
